A three man committee to make recommendation about fluoridation. What a gimmick to foist upon the citizens! The dentist-commissioner is FOR it without any conference. Besides, he is gag-bound by Section 20 Code of Ethics, ADA not to publicly oppose ADA policies. The physician knows nothing first hand about the effects of fluoridated water over a long period of time on human bodies. His "study" will consist of reading USPHS material. ("To tell the public that any of these programs are all right, but that there may be some undesirable side effects, is another sure way to defeat the program. The present standards were achieved by telling the public DEFINITELY AND EMPHATICALLY what they should do, and this is exactly what must be done with the present fluoridation program if the public is to adopt it." - Bull, PHS in Journal ADA, Feb, 1952. P. 149). The navy man presumably is biased. The paper has indicated the Navy would go along with the program.

If the Committee recommends fluoridation - then what? An opinion held by three men carries no more power or authority to force tooth decay treatment on citizens than would similar opinion from any other three or three thousand men from either high or low places. Scientists, pseudo-scientists, dentists and physicians are privileged to make findings but citizens are not legally bound to use these findings on their bodies. The U. S. Constitution gives them the privilege of being secure in their homes and bodies by freedom of choice.

Sincerely yours,

d. e. Menedez
1928 Nebraska Avenue

Tampa, Florida

A possible tax rate increase of 1.5 to 4.0 cents is the current outlook for Montgomery County homeowners, the Montgomery County Taxpayers, Inc. said to-day.

In a gloomy bulletin, Morris Allen, executive director of the group, forecast an 8 to 18 per cent increase in the present assessment-disclosures rate. The outlook, he said, was based on indications of present budget request plans and estimates of the county departmental heads.

Mr. Allen said the exact increase would depend on these requests, the budget-cutting ability of County Manager E. T. Beall and the county council's efforts to trim Mr. Beall's recommendations.

Other Factors.

The amount of new property put on the tax books, increased revenues, and the public's attitude also will be determining factors, Mr. Allen said.

The director said the biggest potential budget increase lies in the school board's anticipated request for from $1.5 million to $2.2 million over the present $8.1 million.

The lion's share of this increase will go toward the hiring of 150 to 200 more teachers, so other employees, and higher pay scales recently adopted by the board.

Mr. Allen also forecast a $100,000 to $1 million hike in the requests from other county departments which spend about $4.5 million. The major share of this increase will go for hiring more policemen, assessors, nurses and for higher pay scales for police and other county employees, he said.

$100,000 Jump Seen.

The present $5 million debt service which is used to meet obligations on the county's bonded indebtedness is expected to jump $100,000 to $200,000, Mr. Allen said.

The overall increase in the budget, based on current departmental request plans and estimates will be from $2.3 million to $3.5 million over the present $15.6 million.

Mr. Allen, however, said the potential net increase in revenues at present is expected to amount to $1 million to $1.3 million. This would pick up enough of the slack, he said, so that the tax rate increase would be held to 1.5 to 4.0 cents before any cuts are made in the requests of department heads.

The taxpayers group, self-appointed watchdog over the county purse, is composed largely of income-producing property.

The county's expense budget recommendations are due from the county manager by May 11. The council will hold public hearings on the manager's budget in mid-June and then adopt a budget for the new fiscal year beginning July 1.
